title: Telling and asking
goal: Form commands by dropping *å* and *-r* at once, then soften them into requests that sound Norwegian — not a word-for-word copy of English.
bekal: form a command from any base form
forbid with *ikke* placed in front of the command
wave: Review **unit 11** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. Say the eight movement/place pairs once more.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kom inn!
dialogs.intro: Saturday evening at Ahmad's apartment. Budi knocks on the door carrying a plastic bag that is making suspicious noises.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Kom inn! Ta av deg skoene, er du snill.
lines.id: Come in! Take your shoes off, please.
lines.literal: come in! take off you shoes-the, are you kind.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Selvfølgelig. Hvor skal jeg legge jakka?
lines.id: Of course. Where do I put my jacket?
lines.literal: naturally. where shall I put jacket-the?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Heng den der. Og sett deg — maten er nesten klar.
lines.id: Hang it over there. And sit down — the food is almost ready.
lines.literal: hang it there. and seat you — food-the is almost ready.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Gjerne. Kutt løken, men ikke gråt.
lines.id: Sure. Cut the onion, but don't cry.
lines.literal: gladly. cut onion-the, but not cry.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: For sent. Har du et glass vann?
lines.id: Too late. Do you have a glass of water?
lines.literal: for late. have you a glass water?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Ta det selv. Ikke spør meg om alt.
lines.id: Get it yourself. Don't ask me about everything.
lines.literal: take it self. not ask me about everything.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kunne du gi meg et håndkle, da?
lines.id: Could you give me a towel, then?
lines.literal: can you give me a towel, then?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Vær så god. Ikke tørk øynene med den — den er skitten.
lines.id: Here you go. Don't wipe your eyes with it — it's dirty.
lines.literal: be so good. not wipe eyes-the with it — it is dirty.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Smak på maten først. Så snakker vi om det.
lines.id: Taste the food first. Then we'll talk about it.
lines.literal: taste on food-the first. then talk we about it.

notes: **A command is made by dropping two things at once: the word *å* and the ending *-r*.** *å komme* → **kom!**, *å ta* → **ta!**, *å sette* → **sett!**, *å kutte* → **kutt!** What's left is the bare verb, and it really is the shortest form there is.

**Verbs ending in a double consonant lose one**: *å komme* → *kom*; *å sette* → *sett* keeps both because a final *tt* is allowed; *å hjelpe* → *hjelp*. Rough rule: drop the final *-e* and leave the rest.

**A prohibition puts *ikke* in front of the command**: *ikke gråt!*, *ikke spør!*, *ikke tørk!* The command is the only place in all of Norwegian where *ikke* comes before the verb — and the order happens to match English "don't" exactly.
**Er du snill** literally means "if you're kind" and works like a tag "please" at the end of an English sentence. It softens a command without changing its form.

**Sett deg** means "sit down" — literally "seat yourself". This group of verbs that require a reflexive pronoun is unpacked in unit 18; for now learn the three most common: *sett deg* (sit down), *skynd deg* (hurry up), *kos deg* (enjoy yourself).

**Ta av deg skoene** — taking your shoes off when you enter a home is a firmly held custom in Norway, even at a close friend's place. Walking in with shoes on is something Norwegians notice but rarely comment on.

grammars.title: Forming commands
body: One move: drop *å*, drop the *-e* if there is one. No ending is added, and the form is the same for one person or many.
after: The command form doesn't change with the number of people. *Kom!* is used for one person or a whole class — unlike Spanish, French or Arabic, which have different forms. Just like English.
If the verb has a particle, the particle goes after it: *stå **opp**!*, *spis **opp**!*, *kom **inn**!*, *ta **av** deg skoene!*
⚠️ *Å være* has the command form **vær**, and almost the only place you'll meet it is in *vær så snill* (please) and *vær så god* (here you go). Those two phrases have practically frozen the form.

grammars.title: Forbidding
body: This is the only pattern in all of Norwegian where *ikke* comes before the verb — and it happens to match English "don't …" exactly.
after: Compare the last three rows: *ikke ta den!* is a direct order, *la være å ta den* is softer, and *du må ikke ta den* states a rule. All three forbid, at three levels of firmness.
*La være* literally means "let it be" and is used a lot by parents with children — something like "stop that, don't".

grammars.title: From command to request
body: Norwegian has no word for "please" used as often as the English one. Politeness is handled by sentence form, and this table runs from the flattest to the most polite.

head: Norsk
How polite
English
rows: Can you pass me the salt?
Could you pass me the salt?
Could I possibly have the salt?
*Vær så snill å gi meg saltet.*
Please, please pass me the salt.

after: The fourth and fifth rows are the ones you'll need most in daily life — at the checkout, at the office, in someone's home. Learn both as whole phrases.
⚠️ Don't use *vær så snill* in every sentence. English speakers bring their "please" habit here, and the result sounds like begging. Norwegian treats *kan du…?* as fully polite already.

sections.title: In the kitchen and at the table

blocks.text: Commands are heard most often in the kitchen, so this unit's vocabulary gathers there.

head: Norsk
English
rows: Send meg saltet, er du snill.
Fry the fish for ten minutes.

blocks.text: **Takk for maten** must be said every time you finish a meal in a Norwegian home, without exception — to the host, to your mother, to your roommate. Skipping it is really noticed, even though no one will call you out.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Take ten verbs from unit 7 and make all of them into commands, out loud. Then forbid all of them.
Write your favorite recipe in Norwegian, entirely in commands. This is a surprisingly effective exercise, because recipes really are written that way.
Finally, turn five blunt commands into polite requests using the levels in the table on the previous page.
Can I have a glass of water?
